item.content:encoded:
The best time for baseball failure Mike Elias to trade one of his failing former top draft picks is, invariably right now.
Because the longer they persist in his laughingstock player development strata – and the more they toil under what’s been a disaster medical and training staff - invariably their future value will decline and things will only get worse. Among Elias’s superpowers, wrecking top prospects is right up there with building third-grade rosters, hiring inane managers and constructing teams incapable of catching the ball or executing baseball fundamentals.
Which brings us to Jackson Holliday, Elias’s second first-overall selection (with his overt tank forcing even the craven and cynical billionaires who run baseball to change their draft rules), and why he needs to go this offseason. And to be clear Holliday needs to go ASAP as badly as Elias’s first overhyped first-overall pick, Adley Rutschman, needed to be jettisoned before the trade deadline. Long a Holliday skeptic myself – I begged and pleaded them to make him a cornerstone inn a Tarik Skubal package back in 2024 - I tried to keep an open mind that sweeping midseason stance and swing corrections might turn him around, but that was folly.
It’s time for him to be packaged (ideally with failed fifth-overall pick Colton Cowser as should have happened at the deadline) this winter.
This won’t get better here, and we have to operate now with the known constraints moving forward” Elias is as empowered as ever, overmatched puppet skipper Craig Albernaz is back for 2027, and the idea these mooks are going to turn Holliday into a winning centerfielder is ridiculous (though several top analysts believe it can be done). They couldn’t turn him into a competent second baseman after perpetual grifter Elias sold you he was a five-tool All Star shortstop when he drafted him.
Again, I watched him throughout the minors, called this out as an overhyped positionless prospect and begged them to sell him on him when the roster was a Skubal away from doing potential October damage. Alas, those days are gone and they’re not coming back.
Why Now?
So with the two-headed monster of Elibernaz (actually, let’s be real, it’s Albi-ass) coming back, and another Holliday offseason and/or spring training cut short due to surgery (pending wrist procedure) and him slight and brittle and unable to turn his natural speed into any kind of weapon and with him downright deficient at second base, he has to go.
With Jordan Westburg coming back from his latest surgery, and him brittle and not durable, but with a legit run-production profile this lineup desperately needs, he will be given every chance to bounce back. And at this point, I’m simplifying his program – Westburg is a second baseman. Less strain on the body there. Let’s get 120 games out of him there and some DH work.
Because we also know Elias is going to be all about Christian Encarnacion-Strand in 2027, loving to try to turn a AAAA guy into a regular, and with CES’s power productivity and the glove playing better than expected, he is in the mix. And Pete Alonso and Samuel Basallo block first base. Coby Mayo was the one young player who truly exceeded expectations on this roster, and he kills left-handed pitching and you can live with the glove at third once or twice a week.
And Gunnar Henderson is not an MLB shortstop and he won’t be here past the trade deadline and he could be dealt this winter (and they don’t have the guts to move him to third, where he’s always belonged). If he is dealt before the lockout, Blaze Alexander would be an option at short, and they should go get a glove-first shortstop anyway and stop running fake teams out there with no spine. Either way, Elias will want Alexander to play a lot, so you tell me where Holliday fits in?
What About Selling Low?
Never stopped Elias before, it’s another specialty of his, and it could always get worse. In Birdland, it always does. That's The Elias Way.
Holliday has too many voices in his head, and yet another new hitting staff that is surely on the way here as Elias scapegoats middle managers while being a 100% fraud himself, will only make it worse. I’m thinking his daddy is ready for him to have a fresh start (with a team further from alleged contention than the Orioles) and agent Scott Boras is ready for him to have a fresh start, where the pressure of being the overhyped 1-1 won’t matter as much.
We won’t belabor the point defensively, because it’s ugly all around and the instincts at 2B are not natural or fluid. He is 20th among all MLB players with at least 500 innings at second in fielding run value. He is in the 88th percentile in sprint speed and played nearly 100 games this season and had eight steals and got thrown out three times; in an era where they made stealing bases easier than ever, he has 29 steals to 14 times caught stealing for his career.
Abject failure they couldn’t fix this, but a smart organization probably can.
As for the hit tool, man, it’s still a mess. You could tell me he’ll still only be 23 by spring training, but he has 1100 MLB plate appearances and he’s also been in this org five years now and he is going backwards, rapidly. Injuries or not, he had a .640 OPS this season and he was 17 percent worse than the average MLB hitter (OPS+) … those are below his career totals (.654 OPS and 86 OPS+).
Holliday stopped swinging as hard and moved off the plate in the box and changed his swing plane in an effort to get on base more and work the ball between the gaps .. and ended up with a .300 OBP, much worse than last year, and a .229 average, also much worse than 2025. And really, the fact he ends the season on the IL like he began it, needing yet another procedure, kind of says it all.
He is a number nine hitter in a real MLB lineup, and I’m not sure where he plays most of the time. They gave him another run at the top of the lineup when he was hot in July, and that leadoff stint was largely a disaster (.267 OBP and .614 OPS). He had an amazing July, and arguably in every other month he looked like someone who needed more seasoning in AAA.
Holliday had a .582 OPS in 50 games at Camden Yards, a park that should suit him from the left side, and a .601 OPS in the second half of the season. It’s over here.
Sadly, it never even ever really got going here, and worst of all, the guy who created this problem is still the one charged with fixing it.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29

Ceddanne Rafaela’s first game back from the 10-day injured list (right quad strain) lasted all of two innings before the Red Sox removed him for seemingly precautionary reasons.
Boston’s Gold Glove center fielder caught all three outs in the top of the first, even laying out for a diving catch of Cleveland Guardians’ Steven Kwan’s leadoff line drive.
But when Rafaela singled to lead off the bottom of the second, he grimaced as he ran and seemed to pull up lame on first base. He leaned over briefly as he stood on the bag, prompting a visit from manager Chad Tracy and a team trainer. After a few minutes’ discussion and some test running down the first base line, they allowed Rafaela to remain in the game.
Rafaela appeared to run normally as he advanced to second when Caleb Durbin reached first on a fielding error by third baseman José Ramírez, and initially remained on the field after the Red Sox failed to score in the bottom of the second. But Jarren Duran replaced him in center before the top of the third began.
“Just saw him continuing to flex it,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy told ESPN’s Buster Olney moments later on the game broadcast. “That’s all. He seemed to have felt some cramping in the back there. When he went back out there, he kept flexing it, so we said, let’s go ahead and make the change.”
Red Sox media relations announced Rafaela left the game with “right hamstring tightness” two innings later.
The Red Sox already planned to monitor Rafaela’s workload in Wednesday’s game, as the end of the Triple-A season on Sunday meant he returned without playing in single a rehab game.
“You guys know, every ball that gets hit up in the air in his direction, he thinks he can catch it,” Tracy said pregame. “So if you have a very normal, easy game flow, I think he’d be just fine. If you have a game flow where he tracks down seven balls in the gap and hits two doubles, you might say that’s enough.
“We’ll be very reactive to what the game is requiring of him and do our best to make sure we keep him in a good spot.”
Rafaela’s departure had consequences for the Red Sox almost immediately. They loaded the bases in the bottom of the third on back-to-back singles by Roman Anthony and Nick Sogard, and a two-out single by Adley Rutschman. Duran, batting in Rafaela’s No. 6 spot in the order, struck out swinging to end the inning.

The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

BALTIMORE -- Every season, one Baltimore player receives the Most Valuable Oriole Award, an honor that is voted on by members of the local print and broadcast media who cover the team on a regular basis. And some years, it can be a difficult decision resulting in a close race.
That was not the case in 2026.
Pete Alonso was unanimously named the winner of this year’s Most Valuable Oriole Award, the club announced Wednesday. The 31-year-old slugger was the runaway favorite for the recognition, as he was clearly the team’s top player during his first season in Baltimore.
Ballots included up to three players, with points tabulated in a 5-3-1 format (for first, second and third, respectively). The other O’s players to receive votes this year were utility man Blaze Alexander, catcher Samuel Basallo, right-hander Shane Baz, right-hander Kyle Bradish, infielder Christian Encarnacion-Strand, right-hander Rico Garcia, shortstop Gunnar Henderson, infielder Coby Mayo, left-hander Trevor Rogers and right-hander Brandon Young.
But nobody was coming close to Alonso, who has lived up to lofty expectations since signing a five-year, $155 million deal to join the Orioles last December.
Alonso has been racking up honors of late, as he was the Orioles’ nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award and also their recipient of the Heart & Hustle Award. Now, he’s the Most Valuable Oriole -- the first unanimous winner since outfielder Cedric Mullins in 2021 -- and it wouldn’t be surprising if he finishes quite high in American League MVP Award voting after his strong conclusion to the season.
Entering Wednesday, Alonso led Baltimore in hits (156), runs scored (94), home runs (40), RBIs (108), batting average (.265), slugging percentage (.510) and OPS (.869). He’s also the only O’s player to start all 157 games this season.
All of the numbers are impressive. But Alonso’s power and run production have stood out most.
Now sitting at 304 career home runs, Alonso has clubbed at least 37 homers in six of his eight MLB seasons and has reached the 40-homer mark four times. The Polar Bear is the ninth player in Orioles history (since 1954) to hit 40 in a season, marking the 10th overall occurrence.
Alonso’s 108 RBIs are the most in the AL. He is on pace to become the first player in AL/NL history to post a season in which he led the league in RBIs in both leagues. (Alonso had a National League-high 131 RBIs for the Mets in 2022.)
The stats have never been the most important thing to Alonso, though.
“I just want to leave it all out there,” Alonso recently said. “I really love playing the game, and for me, I just want to be all I can be and do whatever I can every single night to win the game, you know? I really take pride in wanting to win and giving it all I have.”
The Orioles (76-81 entering Wednesday) are unlikely to reach the postseason, as they’re close to elimination. But Alonso has four more years remaining on his contract and is hopeful he can lead the club back to the playoffs as soon as possible.
Players to win MVO in first season with Orioles
OF Chuck Diering (1954)
OF Dave Philley (1955)
RHP Stu Miller (1963)
OF Frank Robinson (1966)
OF Ken Singleton (1975)
RHP Rodrigo Lopez (2002, rookie)
SS Miguel Tejada (2004)
DH Nelson Cruz (2014)
C Adley Rutschman (2022, rookie)
1B Pete Alonso (2026)
Alonso has hit well, played strong defense at first base and become a leader inside Baltimore’s clubhouse. He’s been an even better fit with the O’s than those in the organization could have imagined he’d be this past winter.
“My belief on any long-term contract is, if you’re going to do anything over three years -- especially when you get into the five-year, 10-year range -- that person has to have behaviors that impact the environment. You want that guy to have a compound effect where he gets people better,” bench coach Donnie Ecker said. “Pete’s up there with the best I’ve seen, just in terms of caring for the people around him and really not ever settling for average.”

BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots on Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith recorded the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits.

item.content:encoded:
For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
“He’s working through stuff,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said postgame of Miller. “I thought today was even another step in the right direction, the hit batter, the free passes are what gets you and I think he also got some bad batted ball (luck).”
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie regular season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
When Tolle next takes the mound, it will most likely be at Yankee Stadium to start a game in the AL Wild Card Series.
“I’m really proud of this group,” Tolle said. “I’ve had so much fun obviously with these guys and to continue to go into the postseason with them and I’m really excited about us.”
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs. Miller said postgame that he felt less comfortable on Tuesday than he had the last time out in Tampa Bay, but while his patience is wearing thin the only way to overcome his struggles is by pitching through them.
“I would like to have been through this by now and be over it but all I can do is keep taking the ball and get through it,” Miller said. “There’s no way I can feel better and get through without throwing in games so that’s how it’s going to have to be, just keep throwing and get through it.”
As for what he hopes to see from his club over the last week, Tracy said the big thing is keeping everyone healthy and engaged.
“You’re still working on timing, you’re still working on things with your swing, so all of that matters,” Tracy said, adding that the other big priority is being proactive with the pitching staff. “Looking at it before the game, who do we want available today, being strict to it and trying to get the guys in the bullpen the work that they need but still being competitive in that game. So there’s a lot of things that you’re doing.
“I told the guys before we earned the right to be in a position to line things up, but that being said we still want to go out and win games,” Tracy continued. “We had a chance to do that tonight, we did some things well, I think we were (0 for 9) with runners in scoring position, so we had our chances.”
Rafaela expected back
Following the game Tracy said he expects Ceddanne Rafaela will be activated from the injured list on Wednesday. Willson Contreras still has some soreness in his hand and won’t return to the lineup but is getting closer, and Tracy confirmed Trevor Story was given a scheduled day off to give him some rest ahead of the playoffs.
Aroldis Chapman, who has been dealing with some lat tightness, may also be ready to return to action on Wednesday as well, though Tracy said they’ll want to make sure he feels good pregame before making that call.

BOSTON (AP) — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim first-place lead in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who hold a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the Central and have won six straight. Chicago, which won 14-11 over Kansas City, owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded a season-high for a nine-inning game of 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits. In his previous start on Sept. 13, he had Boston’s second recorded immaculate inning that opened a game.
Up next
Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) is set to face Red Sox RHP Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82) on Wednesday in the middle game of the three-game series.

The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

The Baltimore Orioles, under failed head of baseball operations Mike Elias, are incapable of cultivating their greatest resources into consistently productive players.
Since running off one of the most respected and accomplished training staffs so Elias could bring in his own people, their Injured List stints have soared and the same recurring injuries have cropped up and their most important young everyday players have regressed, markedly and quickly, and, in some cases, perhaps permanently. So watching 22-year-old catcher Samuel Basallo struggle mightily and not look like himself and appear to be compensating for a lingering shoulder injury deep into a lost season is a major concern for him (especially against the backdrop of what has become of Gunnar Henderson and Jackson Holliday, among others).
Wasn’t that long ago that Basallo was the most prodigious power hitting catcher under the age of 22 in MLB history, as we documented at the time. He also left a game against Toronto briefly back in May wincing and leaving with trainers, only to pop back up in the on deck circle late in the game, only to experience more issues that clownish rookie manager Craig Albernaz tried to minimize,only to end up on the IL in July, after all, with what was deemed “right shoulder inflammation” and struggle mightily ever since.
Carrying three catchers for most of the second half of the season, again, in a lost season, there seemed to be a mounting case for shutting down a young man who ended up catching infinitely more innings for this team than alleged star Adley Rutschman and endured his fair share of adversity in a rookie season at a very young age for someone manning this position. That seemed smart ever before he took a foul tip tot he head Monday that had him getting checked for a concussion.
It seems even more obvious, now.
This kid barely caught 200 games in the minors, and I am thoroughly convinced the shoulder situation has been fairly significant for way longer than they got around to putting him on the IL. Regardless, the second half has been a mess.
Hitting The Wall
Basallo has not seemed comfortable at all since being reactivated and his power stroke is lacking and he’s been getting under the ball a lot and failing to line things up. His strikeout rate has gone from 26% to 30%.
Split G GS PA HR RBI BA OBP SLG OPS
1st Half 83 70 301 16 46 .248 .309 .464 .772
2nd Half 29 24 98 2 8 .140 .235 .221 .456
In May, as Basallo came into his own, he did what he always did in the minors – destroy fastballs. He hit .314 of fastballs that month and slugged .543. Since then, he is 15-for-100 against fastballs with just five extra base hits (all homers). That’s a massive red flag and I tend to think health and wear and tear have much to do with it. And probably some mounting frustration with one of MLB’s worst hitting staffs that has undermined many a fledgling career already.
Any chances of trying to end this season at anything close to the power and ferocity with which he was swinging the bat in midsummer is long gone. How much first base he ends up playing in the future – or even picking up some right field – remains to be seen. And hopefully he will not need any sort of procedures or clean ups this offseason.

The Boston Red Sox have officially named Chad Tracy as their full-time manager, removing the interim tag and signing him to a three-year contract. Tracy, who is 41 years old, took over the managerial role from Alex Cora on April 26 and has since led the team to a 74-55 record, securing an American League Wild Card berth.
Tracy's leadership has been instrumental in the team's success this season, and his appointment comes as the Red Sox continue to make bold moves under the guidance of Craig Breslow, the team's chief baseball officer. Breslow, known for his willingness to take significant in-season risks, has seen his strategies pay off with the team's second consecutive postseason appearance. On Tuesday (September 22), the Red Sox picked up Breslow's contract options for the 2029 and 2030 seasons, further solidifying his role in the organization.
Breslow's decision to fire Alex Cora and overhaul the coaching staff early in the season was a notable gamble that has since been vindicated. The Red Sox's aggressive approach included the mid-season acquisition of catcher Adley Rutschman and infielder Curtis Mead, moves that have contributed to the team's playoff run. According to the Boston Globe, Breslow emphasized the importance of acting decisively and creating a supportive environment for players to thrive.
As the Red Sox prepare for the postseason, Tracy expressed gratitude to his team, saying, "I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, 'The hell with that, we’re going to the playoffs.'" His leadership and the team's resilience have set the stage for what fans hope will be a successful playoff run.

When you are as bush league an operation as Craig Albernaz’s 2026 Baltimore Orioles, it usually doesn’t take long for your complete lack of fundamentals and remedial-at-best baseball IQ to shine through.
Monday night, starting pitcher Shane Baz issued a leadoff walk on a pitch timer violation, then gave up three runs on three straight pitchers, continuing his ability to focus and command in the first inning, and these baseball losers were on the cusp of clinching yet another losing season under baseball failure exec Mike Elias. Thanks to Pete Alonso they staved off loss No. 82 – don’t worry, it’s coming – and won game No. 75 (they’re better than last year!) in a 4-3 victory over Toronto at a predictably desolate Camden Yards.
Alonso hit an opposite field homer early in the game and Gunnar Henderson delivered a solo homer and Alonso won it for them by clubbing homer No. 40 to left field, a two-run shot that gave them a rare one-run victory. Problem is they are 4.5 games back in the Wild Card and they have five to play, so you do the math.
“Just really stoked I was able to come through for the team right there,” Alonso said on the MASN post-game show.
Baz – as utterly middling of an MLB starter as you will fine who Elias mortgaged what was left of his middling farm system for at the time – showed guts, getting over his poor first inning (that’s been a constant) – and performed well after taking a liner off his elbow last time out. There is a good chance that this trade haunts this organization with 21-year old catcher Caden Bodine already on the Rays taxi squad, but Elias is a human curse so we’ve come to expect no less
So Close To Finally Being Over
Outside of Alonso, hasn’t been much to come to the park to see, yet again, this season. (Rookie catcher Samuel Basallo was for a while but is clearly beat up and getting checked for a concussion after taking a hard foul tip behind the plate Monday).
And with Elias and Albernaz coming back, you can already smell the stench of their 2027 season before it starts, and the propaganda campaign to whitewash this season and try to grift you into spending on next year’s model is well under way.
Does anyone get excited about a team that can catch or run or throw? Do you enjoy watching AAA players all over the place nine years into a rebuild? Let me guess, Albernaz now pretending that getting tough about mistakes made by guys like Rece Hinds and Jeremiah Jackson – who have no business being in MLB, but Elias is so inexplicably horrible at his job they are – doesn’t do it for you?
No problem, MASN went to great lengths Monday to gaslight you about this lost season, and the bumbling clown running the dugout. They run interference and peddle fake talking points about what Henderson has become, pretending he hasn’t tanked as bad as Adley Rutschman did here, and cover for his constant misstep in all aspects of play … And now all of a sudden they’re championing Albernaz’s pathetic rants, 150 games into a lost year, about guys who don’t belong here and are riffing on what a tone he is setting by castrating career minor leaguers.
You aren’t fooling anybody, just demeaning yourselves. Yuck.
Just when you thought you couldn’t lose any more respect for an absolute joke of a franchise, they go and surprise you again by taking their overt PR campaign to another level. There is no bottom with these people and how low they are willing to sink for their paychecks. They all deserve each other. Baltimore deserves so much more.

These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror.
These rankings, as always, are compiled from MLB.com contributors whose names you can find at the bottom of this (and every) piece, but the words are mine. If you dislike the rankings, yell at all of us. But if you dislike the words, feel free to yell at me.
Also, as we close the season, we note for each team the highest they were ranked in our Power Rankings all season -- when they hit the peak.
1. Brewers (previously: 1)
Season High Water Mark: 1, this week
It’s the best season in Brewers history. It sure looks like they’re going to win 100 games for the first time ever. They’ve got a Cy Young frontrunner in Jacob Misiorowski, they’ve got all the momentum, and they’ve got a team that wins by doing all the little things right. Last year was a huge postseason bummer. Now is the time to right that wrong.
2. Dodgers (previously: 2)
Season High Water Mark: 1, Aug. 17
The Dodgers have had a lot of drama this year, much of it revolving around a hugely disappointing first season at Chavez Ravine for Kyle Tucker and injury concerns for Shohei Ohtani. And yet here they are, one of the best teams in baseball, as always, and the team everyone knows is looming in October.
3. Rays (previously: 4)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 25
Don’t forget, almost no one picked the Rays to win the tough AL East this year. But it looks like it’s going to be theirs, with a deep, versatile roster led by Junior Caminero, who looks like he’s going to be a signature star in this league for the next decade-plus.
4. Braves (previously: 3)
Season High Water Mark: 1, June 15
Every year since their World Series title in 2021 has felt a little bit like a disappointment in its own way, even the 104-win season in '23. But this one sure hasn’t, with the Braves overcoming a '25 losing season by winning the division again. And check out Ronald Acuña Jr., who looks like a superstar again.
5. Yankees (previously: 5)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 4
For a long time, it was assumed that if Aaron Judge was hurt for an extended period of time, the Yankees were cooked. But thanks to a fantastic pitching staff -- including Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler -- the Yankees look as strong as ever. But it still may all ride on Judge regardless.
6. Cubs (previously: 6)
Season High Water Mark: 1, May 11
What more can you say about Pete Crow-Armstrong at this point? He’s about to end the Shohei Ohtani MVP reign, and he’s doing so while becoming one of the most popular players in the sport and having one of the best seasons in Cubs history. And it sure feels like October is going to fit him like a glove.
7. Red Sox (previously: 8)
Season High Water Mark: 6, Aug. 5
This season looked absolutely lost in June, and Red Sox fans were tearing their hair out. Then, suddenly, the Sox were playing the best of any team in baseball, and they rode that run all the way to a playoff spot. And it's sure looking like we'll get another installment of The Rivalry in the Wild Card.
8. Padres (previously: 9)
Season High Water Mark: 3, April 20
The Padres have justified all the investments A.J. Preller and company have made in the offseason with this late-season run, but they still have won just one game past the Division Series round this century. The top of the NL is tough this year, but no one’s hotter than the Padres.
9. Phillies (previously: 7)
Season High Water Mark: 5, July 16
It has been a rocky road, with Don Mattingly taking over early in the season, the team righting itself, and then struggling down the stretch. But in this ear, all that matters for the Phillies is the postseason. All of their questions are about to be answered, one way or the other.
10. Guardians (previously: 12)
Season High Water Mark: 5, June 8
The Guardians’ fight back to the top of the AL Central wasn’t as dramatic as last year’s, but if they can end up atop the division when it’s all said and done, it won’t matter. And if they do … they might just get a first-round bye out of it.
11. White Sox (previously: 11)
Season High Water Mark: 6, June 15
If the White Sox aren’t able to get into the playoffs after the fun season they’ve had, it will feel like a heartbreaker, but it probably shouldn’t be. This is a team that has lost 100-plus games for three consecutive seasons! Look at where they are now! The playoffs would be wonderful. But what a major step forward they’ve made. With more to come.
12. Rangers (previously: 16)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 3
The Rangers have never gotten higher than three games over .500 this year … but that has not kept them out of the middle of the AL West, and even atop the division. They’ve only made the playoffs once in the last decade -- the year they won the World Series. That may well change this season.
13. Diamondbacks (previously: 10)
Season High Water Mark: 9, Aug. 17
The Padres’ torrid run down the stretch may end up keeping Arizona out of the playoffs, though the season’s final series between the two teams could have something to say about that. But a year of uncertainty ended up being a positive one, despite some off-field drama … and there’s still time left in this one.
14. Astros (previously: 13)
Season High Water Mark: 7, April 6
Yordan Alvarez had a fully healthy season and responded with an all-timer of an offensive performance. The only question now is whether they can catch the intrastate-rival Rangers for the AL West crown -- and it looks like they're going to have to, if they want to make the playoffs at all.
15. Blue Jays (previously: 14)
Season High Water Mark: 2, March 23
It looked for a while like the Jays, after the brutal way they lost the World Series last year, would make up for a disappointing season by sneaking into the final Wild Card spot. How fans feel about this season may depend on whether or not they can crawl their way back in. It’s going to be an uphill climb.
16. Pirates (previously: 15)
Season High Water Mark: 5, April 20
Pirates fans had big hopes for this year, and while they weren’t the playoff team that some had expected, they nevertheless have won 79 games and could notch their first winning season since 2018. It’s progress.
17. Orioles (previously: 19)
Season High Water Mark: 10, March 23
It may have hurt to do it, but the O’s did maximize their return for Adley Rutschman with even more young players to add to the ones they already have. It’s understandable if O’s fans are skeptical, but you can’t argue that Pete Alonso was a great investment, and really a North Star for the whole franchise at this point.
18. Marlins (previously: 18)
Season High Water Mark: 8, July 16
Take away that 12-game losing streak, and the Marlins are a playoff team this year. You obviously can’t do that, but the different way the Marlins have been doing things started to pay off this year. And they may well have a star in Otto Lopez.
19. Tigers (previously: 21)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 27
This turned out to be their first losing season since 2023, which is frustrating because hopes were so high heading into the year, but there is still a ton of young talent here, led by Riley Greene, who is quietly putting together a stellar start to his career. And with the Tarik Skubal trade, there’s even more young talent on the way.
20. Cardinals (previously: 17)
Season High Water Mark: 8, May 18
The bullpen fell apart down the stretch, making the record look worse than the season felt, but the Cardinals made many steps forward this year, particularly with the lineup: Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez, Alec Burleson and Leo Bernal all look like lineup mainstays … with even more talent coming down the pipe.
21. Nationals (previously: 24)
Season High Water Mark: 12, June 22
James Wood is a star, but he was hardly the only National to emerge in 2026, with CJ Abrams and the recently extended Cade Cavalli setting themselves up as players the Nationals can build around. The offense was terrific this year: That’s the first time you’ve been able to say that in a long time.
22. Mariners (previously: 20)
Season High Water Mark: 3, March 23
So, yeah, it was a bit of a disaster season for the Mariners, in just about every possible way. But this was not a now-or-never season for the M’s: They have a very exciting rotation for 2027, and note that Cal Raleigh started to warm up as the season came to a close as well.
23. Mets (previously: 23)
Season High Water Mark: 5, March 23
That most of the offseason moves blew up in their faces is the reason they’re not in the playoffs, but they certainly played well enough in the second half to look like a playoff team, thanks largely to rookies Carson Benge, A.J. Ewing and Nolan McLean. The Mets will look different next year, but that’s a good thing.
24. Twins (previously: 22)
Season High Water Mark: 15, Aug. 5
The next generation of Twins stars has arrived: Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez all made their debut this year (and still have Rookie of the Year eligibility for next season). This was a transition year for the Twins. There’s plenty of reason to think they can turn the corner in 2027.
25. Reds (previously: 25)
Season High Water Mark: 6, April 27
This was the superstar step forward the Reds have been waiting for from Elly De La Cruz. They no longer have to wonder if he’s ever going to make the leap: He now has. And remember, he is still only 24 years old.
26. Royals (previously: 26)
Season High Water Mark: 14, May 11
Not much went the way it was supposed to this year, but there’s still a lot of young talent here. And there is Bobby Witt Jr., who, even in a down power year (for him), leads the American League in WAR, per FanGraphs.
27. Giants (previously: 27)
Season High Water Mark: 18, March 23
The terrible start, and the occasional discord and chaos, made this season feel like it was over with before it even began. But don’t overlook the fact that Rafael Devers, for most of this season, looked like the superstar the Giants traded for.
28. Angels (previously: 29)
Season High Water Mark: 19, April 20
A potential sale of the team is something that fans have wondered could change the trajectory of this franchise, and they’re going to get the opportunity to find out. There’s some young talent starting to percolate here, perhaps most notably Walbert Ureña, a 22-year-old who looks like he might already be an ace.
29. A’s (previously: 28)
Season High Water Mark: 10, May 11
The onslaught of injuries to their position players made people forget how good this lineup was at some point, and how late in the year they were in contention. As they move closer to their move to Las Vegas, there’s still plenty to build on here … and plenty of reason to have optimism for the future.
30. Rockies (previously: 30)
Season High Water Mark: 27, May 4
It does not look like the Rockies are going to avoid 100 losses this year, alas, marking four straight years with 100-plus losses. But they’ll still be double-digit games better than they were last year, and they’ll do so with a front office that seems, at last, to have a clear plan moving forward.
Voters: Jason Catania, Dan Cichalski, Theo DeRosa, Rick Gold Jr., Jared Greenspan, Will Leitch, Brent Maguire, Travis Miller, Brian Murphy, Arturo Pardavila, Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, Andrew Simon, David Venn, Andy Werle.
